# Introduction and Research Objectives

## Research Background

In an experimental study of rat growth (Box, 1950), rats were assigned to three treatment groups: **Control** (no additive), **Thiouracil**, and **Thyroxin** administered via drinking water. Body weights were recorded across five measurement occasions: **Baseline (Week 0)** through **Week 4**.

Following an accident, three rats were removed from the Thyroxin group, leaving $N = 27$ rats and 135 total observations.

## Research Objective

To determine whether rat body weight differs significantly across treatment groups and measurement occasions, and specifically to evaluate whether growth trajectories over time depend on the treatment received (**Treatment** $\times$ Time Interaction).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Data Preparation and Exploration

```{r load-data}
# Load required libraries
library(nlmm)
library(tidyverse)
library(rstatix)
library(ggpubr)

# Load dataset
data("rats", package = "nlmm")

# Format factor variables with clear labels
rats <- rats %>%
  mutate(
    id = factor(id),
    trt = factor(
      trt,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Control", "Thiouracil", "Thyroxin")
    ),
    time = factor(
      time,
      levels = 0:4,
      labels = c("Week 0", "Week 1", "Week 2", "Week 3", "Week 4")
    )
  )

# Inspect data structure
str(rats)
dim(rats)
knitr::kable(rats)
table(rats$trt)
```

### Guide Question Answer

- **Why is the dataset in long format?**\
  *[The data-set is in long format because there are repeating values found in column one, the subject identifier. ID is necessary is order to compare the changes in a participant as time passes, since the data-set aims to compare weekly changes in weight gain depending on treatment type.]*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2. Descriptive Statistics and Data Visualization

### 2.1 Descriptive Summary

```{r descriptive-stats}
rats %>%
  group_by(trt, time) %>%
  get_summary_stats(y, type = "mean_sd")

```

### 2.2 Visualizations

```{r boxplot}
# Boxplot across time points by treatment group
ggboxplot(
  rats,
  x = "time",
  y = "y",
  color = "trt",
  palette = "jco",
  add = "jitter"
) +
  labs(
    title = "Body Weight Distribution Across Weeks by Treatment",
    x = "Measurement Occasion",
    y = "Body Weight (grams)",
    color = "Treatment"
  )
```

```{r interaction-plot}
# Interaction plot of mean body weights over time
rats %>%
  group_by(trt, time) %>%
  summarise(mean_weight = mean(y), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = mean_weight, color = trt, group = trt)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean Growth Trajectories by Treatment Group",
    x = "Measurement Occasion",
    y = "Mean Body Weight (grams)",
    color = "Treatment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Guide Questions Answers

- **Baseline Highest Average:** *[Control=50kg, Thiouracil=50kg]*
- **Growth Patterns per Group:** *[Control group had a weight gain from between 50kg to over 155kg from weeks 0 to 4, Thiouracil treatment had a weight gain spanning from 50kg to 125kg from weeks 0 to 4, Thyroxin had a weight gain spanning from 50kg to above 155kg from weeks 0 to 4]*
- **Visual Evidence of Interaction:** *[Seen in the interacton plot that there is a positive relationship between weight and time, as time passes, weight increases steadily]*

# 3. Assumption Checking

### 3.1 Normality: Shapiro-Wilk test per cell (trt x time) and Q-Q plots

```{r normality-test}
rats %>%
  group_by(trt, time) %>%
  shapiro_test(y)

ggqqplot(rats, "y", ggtheme = theme_bw()) +
  facet_grid(time ~ trt)
```

### 3.2 Outliers Check

```{r outliers-check}
rats %>%
  group_by(trt, time) %>%
  identify_outliers(y)
```

### 3.3 Homogeneity of Variances: Levene's test at each measurement occasion

```{r levenes-test}
rats %>%
  group_by(time) %>%
  levene_test(y ~ trt)
```

### 3.4 Homogeneity of Covariance Matrices: Box's M test on wide-format data using α = 0.001

```{r box-m-test}
rats_wide <- rats %>%
  pivot_wider(id_cols = c(id, trt), names_from = time, values_from = y)

box_m(rats_wide[, -c(1, 2)], rats_wide$trt)
```

### 3.5 Sphericity Test and Greenhouse-Geisser Correction

```{r sphericity-test}
rats_stat_2WMAnova <- rstatix::anova_test(data = rats, dv = y, wid = id, between = trt, within = time)

rats_stat_2WMAnova$`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity`

# If p > 0.05, sphericity is met (no correction needed)
# Since Mauchly's test yielded a p = 1.41e-17 (p < 0.001) < 0.05, sphericity was violated therefore below is Greenhouse-Geisser correction being applied.
rats_stat_2WMAnova$`Sphericity Corrections`
```

### 4.5 Summary of Assumptions

The majority of the dataset met the assumptions for a mixed-design ANOVA, although on sphericity the Greenhouse-Geisser correction was applied. Normality was met across 14 out of 15 treatment-by-time cells ($p > 0.05$), there was a single data that stood out a bit (in Treatment 3 at Week 1 ($W = 0.789, p = 0.0318$)), although since the Q-Q plots still aligned well overall and mixed ANOVA handles slight normality deviations, this assumption holds. Rat `id = 19` (Treatment 2) had two outliers at Week 1 ($y = 61$) and Week 2 ($y = 78$), although neither was tagged as extreme (`is.extreme = FALSE`), so technically no extreme outliers came from this dataset. Both homogeneity of variances (Levene's test, $p = 0.124\text{–}0.672$) and homogeneity of covariance matrices (Box's M test, $\chi^2(30) = 22.4, p = 0.839$ at $\alpha = 0.001$) were satisfied. Finally, Mauchly's test was significant ($W = 0.011, p = 1.41 \times 10^{-17} < 0.05$), which meant sphericity was violated and the Greenhouse-Geisser correction ($\varepsilon = 0.342$) was applied to the within-subjects ANOVA results.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 4. Mixed-Design Repeated Measures ANOVA

```{r mixed-anova}
# Fit two-way mixed-design repeated measures ANOVA
rats_stat_2WMAnova <- rstatix::anova_test(
  data = rats,
  dv = y,
  wid = id,
  between = trt,
  within = time
)

# Display complete ANOVA output
rats_stat_2WMAnova

# Display Greenhouse_Geisser corrected ANOVA table
rstatix::get_anova_table(rats_stat_2WMAnova)
```

### Interpretation

1. **Main Effect of Treatment (`trt`):** Rat body weight varied significantly across treatment groups overall, $F(2,24)=11.57$, $p<.001$ ($p=.00031$), $\eta_G^2 = .453$. Averaged across all five measurement occasions, mean body weight differed significantly among the Control, Thiouracil, and Thyroxin groups.

2. **Main Effect of Time (`time`):** After applying the Greenhouse-Geisser correction ($\varepsilon=0.342) due to the violation of sphericity, there was a highly significant main effect of time on body weight, F(1.37,32.84)=656.82, p<.001, $\eta_G^2 = .761$, indicating substantial weight change from baseline (Week 0) through Week 4.

3. **Treatment $\Time$ Interaction (`trt:time`):** There was a significant interaction emerged between treatment group and measurement occasion under the Greenhouse-Geisser correction, $F(2.74,32.84)=19.28$, $p<.001$, $\eta_G^2 = .159$. This confirms that the rate and pattern of rat body weight growth across the four weeks depended significantly on the treatment condition, warranting simple main effects decomposition below.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5. Post Hoc Analysis and Interaction Decomposition

### 5.1 Treatment Differences per Week

Simple one-way ANOVAs and Tukey's HSD pairwise comparisons were performed to determine whether significant differences existed among treatment groups at each observation week.

```{r treatment-differences}
weeks <- levels(rats$time)

for (wk in weeks) {

  cat("\n====================================\n")
  cat("RESULTS FOR", wk, "\n")
  cat("====================================\n")

  week_data <- subset(rats, time == wk)

  model <- aov(y ~ trt, data = week_data)

  cat("\nOne-way ANOVA:\n")
  print(summary(model))

  cat("\nTukey's HSD Pairwise Comparisons:\n")
  print(TukeyHSD(model))
}
```

### Interpretation

No significant treatment differences were observed during Weeks 0, 1, and 2. Although Week 2 was close to the 0.05 significance level (p = 0.0599), it was not statistically significant.

Significant treatment differences emerged during Week 3 (p = 0.000678) and Week 4 (p = 0.0000182). Tukey's HSD results showed that Thiouracil differed significantly from both Control and Thyroxin during these later weeks. Control and Thyroxin did not significantly differ.

### 5.2 Time Differences per Treatment

Repeated-measures ANOVAs were conducted separately for each treatment group, followed by Holm-adjusted paired t-tests to determine which observation weeks differed significantly.

```{r time-differences}
rats <- rats[order(rats$trt, rats$id, rats$time), ]

treatments <- levels(rats$trt)

for (t in treatments) {

  cat("\n====================================\n")
  cat("RESULTS FOR", t, "\n")
  cat("====================================\n")

  treatment_data <- subset(rats, trt == t)

  cat("\nRepeated-Measures ANOVA:\n")

  model <- aov(y ~ time + Error(id/time), data = treatment_data)

  print(summary(model))

  cat("\nHolm-Adjusted Paired t-tests:\n")

  pairwise_results <- pairwise.t.test(
    x = treatment_data$y,
    g = treatment_data$time,
    paired = TRUE,
    p.adjust.method = "holm"
  )

  print(pairwise_results)
}
```

### Interpretation

**Control:** Significant changes were observed across time, F(4,36) = 398.8, p < 0.001. All pairwise week comparisons were significant after Holm adjustment.

**Thiouracil:** Significant changes were observed across time, F(4,36) = 225.1, p < 0.001. All pairwise week comparisons were significant after Holm adjustment.

**Thyroxin:** Significant changes were observed across time, F(4,24) = 160.9, p < 0.001. All pairwise week comparisons were significant after Holm adjustment.

### 5.3 Overall Interpretation

The simple main effects analyses showed that treatment differences were not significant during Weeks 0, 1, and 2 but became significant during Weeks 3 and 4. In particular, the Thiouracil group differed significantly from the Control and Thyroxin groups during the later observation weeks.

Meanwhile, all three treatment groups showed significant changes over time. These findings suggest that the treatment trajectories diverged over the five-week period, particularly involving the Thiouracil group.
